 Ben Shelton shows plenty of power, but still has room for improvement
 Ben Shelton impresses with his serve in his first-round match in Basel
 Keystone
 Jérôme Kym faces a particularly tough challenge in the round of 16 at the Swiss Indoors: He’ll take on top-seeded American Ben Shelton, one of the breakout players of the year.
 Keystone-SDA 
 Today at 05:01 It was a tough match for a first-round contest: It took three tiebreaks and 2 hours and 40 minutes for Shelton to defeat his compatriot Aleksandar Kovacevic, who is ranked 80 places lower in the world rankings. A key factor in his success at Basel’s St. Jakobshalle was his serve. Shelton fired off 44 aces, compared to his opponent’s 13.
 “I’m pretty excited,” Shelton says when asked about this outstanding result. He started the indoor season with the goal of improving his serve. “We tweaked the technique a bit, and I’m trying to serve with more precision rather than speed.” He’s pleased that he’s been so successful with this approach. After all, “that’s how you win on fast indoor courts.”
 Highs and lows alternate
 The tournament in Basel comes six weeks after he reached his first Grand Slam final. At the US Open, Shelton made it to the final—in part thanks to an epic five-set victory over Carlos Alcaraz—but ultimately lost to Alexander Zverev. This feat propelled the left-hander to No. 4 in the world rankings—his highest ranking ever.
 "They were the best two weeks I've ever had at a tournament," the 24-year-old said ahead of his match in Basel. He nearly capped off an already impressive year with four tournament victories on three different surfaces. “Still, I see a lot of room for improvement,” said Shelton. The Atlanta-born pro continues to struggle with consistency. This is particularly evident at the Grand Slam tournaments: quarterfinals at the Australian Open, second round at the French Open, first round at Wimbledon, and then his breakthrough in New York.
 However, even after their latest victory, Shelton seemed to have hit a bit of a slump. Before the game against Basel, they had lost three of their last four games.
 With His Father as Coach
 “I think there are still many areas where I can improve,” says Ben Shelton. He can count on the support of a very special coach: his father, Bryan, who was a professional tennis player himself and reached No. 55 in the ATP world rankings in the early 1990s.
 The secret to the success of this partnership is no mystery. “He knows how to work with me, what he should or shouldn’t say at certain moments, and how to motivate me,” says Ben Shelton about his 60-year-old father. Together, they thoroughly analyze the statistics after games to identify weaknesses in Shelton’s play and address them specifically.
 So while Ben Shelton could celebrate his 44 aces against Kovacevic, the 31 unforced errors (Kovacevic: 13) are likely to give him and his father pause for thought.
 He’ll need to cut that lead against Kym—even though Shelton is the clear favorite against the player from Aargau (ATP 222). If he does, Shelton could finally celebrate a title in Basel two years after his surprising loss in the final to Giovanni Mpetshi Perricard.
